text: Vector Store 4.2 changes how the indexer merges on-disk segments during background compaction. Previously, merge candidates were selected purely by segment age, which sometimes combined a large segment with several tiny ones and produced an uneven size distribution across the index. The new selection heuristic instead ranks candidates by a combined score of age and byte size, favoring merges that keep resulting segments close to the configured target size. Early internal benchmarks on a twelve million point collection showed compaction wall-clock time dropping by roughly eighteen percent, with no measurable change in query latency during the merge window.
author: R. Vasquez

text: This release adds a configurable ceiling on the indexer's in-memory segment build buffer, exposed as `indexer.build_buffer_mb` in the deployment configuration. Operators running dense collections with many concurrent writers had reported occasional out-of-memory terminations when several large segments were being built at once. Setting an explicit ceiling causes the indexer to spill partially built segments to a temporary directory once the buffer fills, trading a small amount of extra disk I/O for predictable memory usage. The default ceiling is conservative and should be raised only after confirming the host has adequate free memory headroom.
author: R. Vasquez

text: A long-standing bug where a freshly created payload index could return stale results for a few seconds after creation has been fixed in this release. The root cause was that the indexer's internal cache of field schemas was refreshed on a fixed timer rather than being invalidated immediately when a new index was registered. Index creation now publishes an explicit invalidation event that every indexer worker consumes before serving the next read, closing the window entirely. Teams that previously worked around this by sleeping briefly after index creation calls can remove that workaround.
author: R. Vasquez

text: The legacy `indexer.legacy_flush_mode` flag introduced two releases ago is now deprecated and will be removed in version 5.0. It was originally added to preserve the older, less efficient flush behavior during the migration to the current segment format, and telemetry from the last two quarters shows fewer than half a percent of deployments still rely on it. Operators still setting this flag explicitly should remove it from their configuration files ahead of the next major upgrade; the modern flush path has been the default and recommended setting since version 4.0.
author: R. Vasquez

text: Vector Store 4.5 raises the default number of parallel segment-build threads the indexer spawns during a bulk load from two to four on hosts with eight or more cores. Internal load testing against a twenty million point ingest job showed the higher thread count cut total indexing time by close to a third on suitably sized hardware, while adding only a modest bump in peak CPU utilization. Deployments running on smaller instances can restore the previous behavior by setting `indexer.build_threads` explicitly, which remains fully supported and unaffected by this default change.
author: S. Patel

text: This release fixes a rare race condition in the indexer that could leave a shard split half-finished if the coordinating node restarted mid-operation. The split process now writes a durable checkpoint record before handing ownership of the new shard to a replica, so a restarted coordinator can detect the in-progress split and resume it from the last completed step instead of leaving orphaned shard metadata behind. Two customers hit this condition during planned maintenance windows before the fix, and both cases have been retroactively confirmed resolved against the patched build.
author: S. Patel

text: A new gauge, `indexer_pending_merge_bytes`, is now exported for every collection and reports the total size of segments waiting for background compaction. Operators previously had no direct signal for compaction backlog and had to infer it indirectly from rising segment counts or degraded query latency. The new gauge makes it straightforward to alert when compaction is falling behind sustained write volume, well before the backlog becomes large enough to affect read performance, and is documented alongside the existing indexer metrics in the monitoring reference.
author: S. Patel

text: On the morning of February 8th, write latency to the indexer rose from a typical twenty milliseconds to over four seconds for approximately fifty minutes, affecting every collection hosted on the affected node group. The first customer-visible symptom was a spike in ingest timeout errors reported by three tenants running high-volume batch loads simultaneously. On-call engineers were paged automatically once the write latency service level objective breached its threshold, and the incident was declared within six minutes of the first alert firing.
doc_title: Incident Report: Elevated Write Latency in Indexer
author: R. Vasquez

text: Investigation traced the cause to the write-ahead log queue exhausting its allotted memory buffer after a coordinated spike in ingestion throughput from the three tenants landed within the same thirty second window. Once the buffer filled, every subsequent write had to wait for queued entries to flush to disk before it could be accepted, and the resulting lock contention on the queue's internal mutex compounded the slowdown far beyond what the raw disk throughput alone would explain. No data was lost; every accepted write remained durable throughout the incident.
doc_title: Incident Report: Elevated Write Latency in Indexer
author: R. Vasquez

text: The immediate mitigation was to temporarily throttle ingest throughput for the three affected tenants at the gateway layer, which relieved pressure on the write-ahead log queue within about ninety seconds and allowed the backlog to drain. Once queue depth returned to normal, throttling was lifted gradually over the following ten minutes while latency was monitored closely to confirm the recovery was stable before fully restoring throughput limits to their standard values.
doc_title: Incident Report: Elevated Write Latency in Indexer
author: R. Vasquez

text: Follow-up work includes raising the default write-ahead log buffer size for high-throughput node groups and adding a dedicated alert that fires when buffer occupancy crosses seventy percent, well ahead of the point where lock contention becomes visible to callers. A longer-term item to make the buffer size dynamically scale with observed ingest rate has been filed separately and is targeted for a future indexer release rather than this incident's immediate remediation window.
doc_title: Incident Report: Elevated Write Latency in Indexer
author: R. Vasquez

text: This runbook describes how to recognize and respond to indexer write latency incidents caused by write-ahead log buffer exhaustion, following the pattern first documented during the February 2023 incident. On-call engineers should use it any time indexer write latency crosses the paging threshold and initial triage points toward the ingest path rather than storage hardware or network issues, since those two other causes require an entirely different investigation path.
doc_title: Runbook: Recovering From Indexer Write Latency Incidents
author: M. Haddad

text: Start by checking the `indexer_wal_buffer_occupancy` gauge for the affected node group; sustained readings above seventy percent strongly suggest the buffer is filling faster than it can flush. Cross-reference this against recent ingest throughput from the tenant dashboard to identify whether one or more tenants have started an unusually large batch load in the preceding few minutes, since concurrent large loads are the most common trigger observed so far.
doc_title: Runbook: Recovering From Indexer Write Latency Incidents
author: M. Haddad

text: If buffer occupancy is elevated, apply a temporary ingest throttle to the highest-volume tenant at the gateway layer using the standard rate-limit override procedure, then watch the buffer occupancy gauge for a return toward baseline within two to three minutes. Do not restart the indexer process as a first response; a restart clears in-memory state but does not address the underlying throughput mismatch and has caused longer outages in past incidents unrelated to this one.
doc_title: Runbook: Recovering From Indexer Write Latency Incidents
author: M. Haddad

text: Escalate to the indexer team if buffer occupancy has not begun declining within five minutes of applying the throttle, since that suggests a cause other than the well-understood throughput spike pattern. Once latency has returned to baseline for at least ten consecutive minutes, lift the throttle gradually rather than all at once, and file a short incident note referencing this runbook so future responders can confirm whether the pattern matches.
doc_title: Runbook: Recovering From Indexer Write Latency Incidents
author: M. Haddad

text: This design note proposes replacing the indexer's fixed-schedule compaction with a load-aware trigger that considers both segment count and current write throughput before starting a compaction pass. The current fixed schedule runs every thirty minutes regardless of load, which wastes CPU cycles compacting a lightly written collection and, conversely, falls behind on collections receiving a sustained heavy write rate that the fixed interval was never sized for.
author: L. Chen

text: The proposed trigger computes a compaction urgency score from the ratio of unmerged segment bytes to total collection size, combined with a decaying average of recent write throughput, and starts a pass whenever the score crosses a configurable threshold. Simulation against six months of production write traffic samples suggests this would reduce total compaction CPU time by roughly a quarter while keeping segment counts within the same bounds as the current fixed schedule.
author: L. Chen

text: A key open question is how aggressively the trigger should react to short, bursty spikes in write throughput versus sustained elevated load, since starting a compaction pass in response to a five-second burst would waste resources without meaningfully reducing segment count. The current proposal averages throughput over a two-minute sliding window specifically to avoid reacting to bursts shorter than that, though this window size is still tunable pending further testing.
author: L. Chen

text: Rollout is proposed as an opt-in flag for one release cycle before becoming the default, giving operators of latency-sensitive collections a chance to validate the new trigger against their own traffic patterns before it affects them automatically. Metrics comparing compaction frequency and CPU time under both strategies will be exposed side by side during the opt-in period to make the comparison straightforward for anyone reviewing the rollout.
author: L. Chen

text: This note outlines a plan for automatic shard rebalancing across indexer nodes when a new node joins a cluster that has grown unevenly over time. Today, rebalancing requires an operator to manually trigger a shard move, and in practice this rarely happens promptly, leaving newly added capacity underused for days or weeks after it becomes available for the cluster to actually schedule work onto.
author: R. Vasquez

text: The proposed rebalancer runs as a low-priority background task that continuously compares each node's shard count and total stored bytes against the cluster average, and schedules a small number of shard moves whenever the imbalance exceeds a configurable tolerance. Moves are rate-limited to avoid saturating inter-node bandwidth, and any move can be paused instantly if the node's read or write latency degrades during the transfer.
author: R. Vasquez

text: Safety is a central concern: a shard move must never leave a shard without at least one fully synchronized replica available to serve reads, so the rebalancer always creates the new replica and confirms it has caught up before removing the shard from its original node. This ordering guarantees availability at the cost of temporarily using more disk space during the transition, which the design note argues is an acceptable tradeoff given how infrequently large rebalances are expected to run.
author: R. Vasquez

text: Vector Store 3.9 introduces a configurable timeout for individual query-engine search requests, addressing feedback from operators who wanted a way to bound worst-case latency for a single slow query without affecting the rest of the collection's traffic. The timeout defaults to thirty seconds and can be overridden per request through the client library's request options, with a clear timeout error returned to the caller rather than a silent partial result being returned instead.
author: A. Okafor

text: This release also improves the query engine's handling of filters that match a very small fraction of the collection by adding an early-exit path once enough candidates satisfying the filter have been found. Previously the query engine always scanned candidate results in a fixed order regardless of filter selectivity, which could waste time examining points that would never pass a highly restrictive filter. Internal testing showed a meaningful latency improvement for queries combining a narrow filter with a large candidate pool.
author: A. Okafor

text: A minor but frequently requested change: the query engine now returns a structured error code, rather than a generic message, when a request references a payload field that has no matching index and the collection is configured to reject unindexed filters outright. This makes it far easier for client applications to detect and surface the specific misconfiguration programmatically instead of pattern-matching on error text returned from the server.
author: A. Okafor

text: Vector Store 5.0 is a major release for the query engine, replacing the internal candidate-scoring pipeline with a version that batches distance computations across multiple queries arriving within the same short time window. On workloads with many concurrent low-latency queries, this batching reduces average CPU time per query by allowing the underlying numeric library to operate on larger matrices instead of many small ones processed one request at a time.
author: D. Almeida

text: The new scoring pipeline is fully backward compatible with existing collections and requires no reindexing; the change is entirely internal to how the query engine processes requests once they arrive. Operators upgrading from 4.x should still review the updated resource sizing guidance, since the batching behavior shifts memory usage patterns slightly compared to the previous per-query processing model, particularly under very high concurrent query volume.
author: D. Almeida

text: Also included in 5.0 is a new query engine setting, `query.max_candidates`, that caps the number of candidate points considered before final scoring, trading a small amount of recall for a hard ceiling on worst-case query cost. This is intended for latency-critical deployments willing to accept a slightly lower recall guarantee in exchange for predictable response times under heavy sustained query load.
author: D. Almeida

text: Between 14:02 and 14:41 on September 9th, the query engine's median response time for one collection rose from roughly forty milliseconds to just under six hundred milliseconds, triggering a burst of client-side timeout errors for a downstream recommendation service. No other collections on the same cluster showed elevated latency during this window, which narrowed the investigation quickly to something specific to that one collection's query pattern that afternoon.
author: L. Chen

text: The cause was identified as an unusually large number of concurrent queries using a complex nested filter that the query planner was evaluating less efficiently than typical filters of similar selectivity, due to how the planner estimated the cost of combining several nested conditions. Under normal query volume this inefficiency was not noticeable, but the recommendation service's traffic pattern that afternoon happened to concentrate an unusually high fraction of its requests on exactly this filter shape.
author: L. Chen

text: Once identified, the affected collection's query planner cache was cleared and re-warmed with corrected cost estimates for nested filter combinations, which restored median latency to baseline within about four minutes. A permanent fix to the planner's cost model for nested filters shipped in the following release, and the recommendation service team was notified of the interim workaround while that fix was in progress.
author: L. Chen

text: This runbook covers the routine health checks operators should run against the query engine after any configuration change or planned maintenance, and describes what a healthy baseline looks like for each check. It is intended to be run manually or wired into a post-deployment verification script that gates a rollout before traffic is fully shifted onto the changed configuration.
author: A. Okafor

text: First, confirm the query engine's per-collection median and ninety-fifth percentile latency metrics are within their historical baseline range for at least five minutes of steady traffic; a persistent shift outside that range after a change is the earliest reliable signal that something in the update affected query performance. Second, issue a small batch of representative sample queries covering common filter shapes and confirm the returned result counts match a known-good snapshot recorded before the change.
author: A. Okafor

text: Finally, check that the query planner cache hit rate has not dropped sharply compared to the pre-change baseline, since a sudden drop often indicates the planner is now generating differently shaped query plans that are not benefiting from cached cost estimates the way the previous configuration did. If all three checks pass, the change can be considered verified from a query engine health perspective.
author: A. Okafor

text: This design note proposes revising the query planner's cost model for combined filter and vector similarity requests, motivated by several incidents where the planner underestimated the cost of evaluating a highly selective filter alongside a broad similarity search. The current model treats filter cost and similarity search cost as independent, which does not capture cases where applying the filter first would dramatically reduce the candidate set the similarity search needs to score.
doc_title: Design Note: Query Planner Cost Model
author: R. Vasquez

text: The proposed model instead estimates the selectivity of each filter clause from sampled statistics maintained per payload index and uses that estimate to decide whether filtering before or after the similarity scoring step will produce a lower total cost. Early prototyping suggests this ordering decision alone accounts for the majority of the latency variance seen across different filter shapes in the incident review conducted last quarter.
doc_title: Design Note: Query Planner Cost Model
author: R. Vasquez

text: Maintaining accurate selectivity statistics without materially slowing down writes is the main engineering challenge: statistics need to be refreshed often enough to remain representative as data changes, but recomputing them from a full scan on every write would be far too expensive. The proposal uses a lightweight reservoir sample updated incrementally on write, refreshed fully only during scheduled compaction passes.
doc_title: Design Note: Query Planner Cost Model
author: R. Vasquez

text: A phased evaluation plan is included: first, shadow the new cost model alongside the existing one in production without acting on its decisions, comparing predicted versus actual query cost across a representative traffic sample; only once the shadow comparison shows consistent improvement would the new model begin actually influencing planner decisions, behind a per-collection opt-in flag that operators enable deliberately.
doc_title: Design Note: Query Planner Cost Model
author: R. Vasquez

text: Vector Store 4.0 introduces batch-level retry for the ingestion pipeline, so a transient failure embedding or writing a single chunk within a large batch no longer requires the caller to resubmit the entire batch from scratch. The pipeline now tracks which chunks within a batch have already been durably written and retries only the remaining ones automatically, up to a configurable retry limit set by the operator.
author: S. Patel

text: This release also adds backpressure signaling from the ingestion pipeline back to calling clients: when the pipeline's internal queue depth exceeds a configurable watermark, subsequent ingest requests receive an explicit retryable response rather than being accepted and queued indefinitely. This change is intended to help client applications apply their own backoff logic before pipeline queue depth grows large enough to affect overall system stability.
author: S. Patel

text: Finally, the ingestion pipeline's batch size limit has been raised from one thousand to five thousand chunks per request, reflecting feedback from customers doing large bulk loads who found the previous limit forced an inconvenient number of separate requests. Very large batches still benefit from being split for parallelism, but the higher ceiling removes an artificial constraint that was not protecting anything the new backpressure signaling does not already handle better.
author: S. Patel

text: Starting at 03:12 on June 17th, the ingestion pipeline began rejecting essentially all incoming write requests with a backpressure error, and the condition persisted for just over two hours before automated remediation restored normal acceptance. Every tenant attempting to write during this window was affected, making this one of the broader-impact incidents recorded this quarter, though no previously accepted data was lost or corrupted during the outage.
author: J. Novak

text: The proximate cause was a batch admission gate that stopped releasing queued batches for processing once the in-memory queue depth crossed its configured ceiling, combined with a downstream embedding worker pool that had been running at reduced capacity since an earlier, unrelated deployment rolled out fewer worker replicas than intended. With fewer workers draining the queue, admission never recovered on its own once it tripped.
author: J. Novak

text: During investigation, engineers identified that the specific config key `ingest.backpressure_watermark_kb` had been left at its conservative default of two thousand rather than being raised alongside the increased traffic the pipeline had grown to handle over the preceding two quarters, meaning the admission gate was tripping at a queue depth far below what the pipeline's actual worker capacity could otherwise sustain.
author: J. Novak

text: Remediation restored the missing embedding worker replicas to their intended count and raised the ingestion pipeline's backpressure threshold to a value consistent with current traffic, after which queued batches drained within roughly fifteen minutes and write acceptance returned to normal. A follow-up item was filed to alert automatically whenever deployed worker replica counts drift from their configured intent, since that drift was the underlying trigger for this incident.
author: J. Novak

text: This runbook explains how to recover the ingestion pipeline when clients report a wave of failed writes that does not clear on its own after a few minutes. It reflects the recovery steps developed during the June 2023 outage and should be the first reference consulted before attempting any manual intervention on the pipeline's intake controls.
author: J. Novak

text: Begin by checking how many loader processes are currently running against the number specified in the deployment manifest; a shortfall here is the most common reason the backlog of failed writes refuses to drain, since fewer active processes means queued work is consumed more slowly than it arrives even after client-side traffic has otherwise returned to normal levels overall.
author: J. Novak

text: If the process count matches expectations but writes are still being rejected, check whether the high-water mark controlling when new work is accepted has kept pace with the pipeline's typical sustained load; a threshold set for an earlier, lower traffic era will trip prematurely and hold the backlog closed longer than the pipeline's real processing capacity requires. Raise the threshold cautiously and confirm queue depth begins falling before considering the incident resolved.
author: J. Novak

text: This note evaluates whether the ingestion pipeline should choose batch sizes dynamically based on observed embedding latency rather than relying on a single fixed batch size configured by the operator. Fixed batch sizes work well for uniform workloads but perform poorly when chunk text length varies widely within the same source, since a batch of unusually long chunks takes far longer to embed than one of short chunks of the same count.
author: D. Almeida

text: The proposed approach estimates a target batch byte budget from a rolling average of recent per-chunk embedding latency, adjusting the number of chunks per batch up or down to keep total estimated batch latency within a stable target range regardless of individual chunk length. Simulation against a corpus with highly variable chunk lengths shows this smooths batch completion time noticeably compared to a fixed chunk-count batch size.
author: D. Almeida

text: A tradeoff worth flagging: dynamic sizing adds a small amount of bookkeeping overhead per batch to track the rolling latency average, and in workloads where chunk length is already fairly uniform this overhead delivers no measurable benefit over the simpler fixed-size approach. The note recommends dynamic sizing be an opt-in feature rather than the default, since the fixed-size approach remains simpler to reason about for the common case.
author: D. Almeida

text: Vector Store 4.3 adds incremental snapshots to the snapshot service, allowing an operator to capture only the segments that changed since the previous snapshot rather than a full copy of the collection every time. For large, slowly changing collections this can reduce both snapshot creation time and the storage consumed by a retained history of snapshots by a substantial margin over a full-copy approach.
author: A. Okafor

text: Restoring from an incremental snapshot chain now requires specifying the full sequence of snapshots back to the last full snapshot, and the snapshot service validates that the chain is complete and unbroken before beginning the restore, refusing to proceed and returning a clear error if any snapshot in the chain is missing. This validation step was added specifically to avoid a partial, silently incomplete restore reaching production traffic.
author: A. Okafor

text: This release also exposes snapshot creation and restore progress as a percentage through the monitoring API, replacing the previous binary in-progress or complete status. Long-running snapshot or restore operations on very large collections had previously given operators no visibility into whether the process was nearly done or barely started, which this change addresses directly for every snapshot operation going forward.
author: A. Okafor

text: During a scheduled disaster-recovery drill on May 2nd, a restore from a snapshot taken the previous night failed partway through with a checksum mismatch error on one segment file, halting the drill and prompting an investigation into whether the underlying snapshot itself was corrupted or whether the failure was specific to the restore process being tested that day.
doc_title: Incident Report: Snapshot Corruption on Restore
author: R. Vasquez

text: Investigation determined that the snapshot service had captured the affected segment file while the indexer was in the middle of rewriting it during a routine compaction pass, producing a snapshot of a file that was neither the old nor the new complete version but an inconsistent mix of both, which is exactly the condition a checksum mismatch is designed to catch before it reaches a restored collection.
doc_title: Incident Report: Snapshot Corruption on Restore
author: R. Vasquez

text: The snapshot service previously coordinated with the indexer only at the collection level, pausing new writes but not confirming that any in-flight segment rewrites had fully completed before capturing files. The fix adds a per-segment completion check to that coordination step, so the snapshot service now waits for any in-progress segment rewrite to finish before including that segment in the snapshot.
doc_title: Incident Report: Snapshot Corruption on Restore
author: R. Vasquez

text: This runbook describes how to verify a snapshot restore completed correctly before declaring a disaster-recovery drill or an actual restore successful, following the gap identified during the May 2022 corruption incident where a restore failure was only caught by chance during a drill rather than by systematic verification of the result.
author: M. Haddad

text: After any restore completes without an explicit error, run the snapshot service's built-in checksum verification pass against every restored segment file before considering the collection trustworthy, even though the restore process itself performs some validation; the built-in pass checks a broader set of file properties than the inline validation the restore path performs by default.
author: M. Haddad

text: Next, compare the restored collection's total point count and per-shard point counts against the values recorded in the snapshot's manifest at capture time. A mismatch here, even without a checksum failure, is a strong signal the snapshot was taken while writes were still in flight and should be treated as a serious enough finding to escalate rather than accept and move on with the drill.
author: M. Haddad

text: If verification fails at either step, do not promote the restored collection to serve production traffic. Instead, escalate to the snapshot service team with the manifest and verification output attached, and attempt the restore again from an earlier snapshot in the retained history while the failed snapshot is investigated separately for the specific coordination issue that might have produced it.
author: M. Haddad

text: Vector Store 4.1 adds support for rotating auth gateway bearer tokens without a restart, so an operator can issue a new token and revoke an old one while the gateway continues serving traffic uninterrupted. Previously, rotating a token required a full gateway restart, which briefly interrupted every client connected through that gateway instance regardless of which token they were actually using at the time.
author: D. Almeida

text: The auth gateway also gains a configurable per-token rate limit in this release, allowing an operator to cap request volume for an individual token independently of the collection-level rate limits already in place. This is intended for deployments issuing separate tokens per downstream team or application, where one team's traffic spike should not be able to degrade service for another team sharing the same gateway.
author: D. Almeida

text: A smaller change: the auth gateway now logs the token label rather than a raw token prefix in its audit log entries, making it far easier to identify which team or application issued a given request without needing to cross-reference a separate token registry. This change required no configuration and applies automatically to every token from this release onward.
author: D. Almeida

text: This design note proposes an automated token rotation schedule for the auth gateway, building on the manual zero-restart rotation capability shipped in 4.1. Manual rotation solved the availability problem but still relies on an operator remembering to rotate tokens periodically, and an informal survey of deployments found most tokens had never been rotated since initial issuance to a team.
doc_title: Design Note: Auth Gateway Token Rotation
author: L. Chen

text: The proposed schedule would let an operator configure a maximum token age, after which the gateway automatically issues a replacement token, notifies the configured owner through the existing alerting integration, and keeps the old token valid for a short grace period to allow the owner to update their client configuration before the old token is finally revoked for good.
doc_title: Design Note: Auth Gateway Token Rotation
author: L. Chen

text: A key design question is how to notify token owners in a way that is neither easy to miss nor so aggressive that teams begin ignoring the notifications entirely; the proposal suggests escalating notification frequency only as the grace period approaches its end, rather than sending an equal volume of reminders throughout the full grace period from the start.
doc_title: Design Note: Auth Gateway Token Rotation
author: L. Chen

text: Security review raised one open concern: automatic rotation must not silently mask a token that should have been revoked for a security reason rather than simply aged out, so the proposal includes a separate, always-manual revocation path that bypasses the grace period entirely and takes effect immediately, clearly distinguished in the audit log from a routine scheduled rotation event.
doc_title: Design Note: Auth Gateway Token Rotation
author: L. Chen

text: This runbook covers how to backfill missing metrics collector data after a gap caused by a collector outage or a misconfigured scrape target, so that dashboards and historical alerting thresholds are not left with a visible hole or a misleading average for the affected period once the collector itself recovers.
author: S. Patel

text: First, confirm the extent of the gap by checking the metrics collector's own internal ingestion log for the affected time range, which records exactly which scrape targets failed and for how long, rather than assuming the gap matches the full duration of the outage that caused it; partial data often still arrived from targets that recovered independently before the rest.
author: S. Patel

text: For gaps under one hour, the standard backfill script can pull raw samples directly from each affected target's local retention buffer, provided the backfill is run before that buffer's own retention window expires and the samples are overwritten. Running the backfill script against a target that is still healthy and reachable is safe and idempotent.
author: S. Patel

text: For longer gaps where the local retention buffer has already rolled over, backfill is not possible and the gap should instead be documented in the metrics collector's known-gaps registry with the affected time range and cause, so that any dashboard or alert relying on data from that period can account for it rather than treating the gap as a genuine zero value.
author: S. Patel
